The Election of 2000. George W. Bush's disputed victory over Al Gore hinged on a five hundred thirty-seven vote margin in Florida and a five-to-four Supreme Court decision that many viewed as a constitutional violation. Gore won the national popular vote by five hundred forty thousand votes but fell short in the Electoral College. Florida's contested results were halted by the Court's Bush v. Gore decision, which stopped the recount and handed the presidency to Bush.

Al Gore, Clinton's vice president, won forty-eight point four percent of the popular vote nationally but lost the Electoral College by four votes. George W. Bush, the Texas governor, won forty-seven point nine percent of the popular vote but claimed Florida's twenty-five electoral votes on the basis of a contested recount. Florida's election was incompetently administered: the butterfly ballot in Palm Beach County confused thousands of voters, and overvoting and undervoting were rampant.

Florida law required a recount when the margin was less than half a percent. The recount exposed hanging chads, pregnant chads, and thousands of ambiguous ballots. Different Florida counties used different standards for counting; by late November, Bush held a five hundred thirty-seven vote margin. Gore's campaign sought a hand recount of disputed counties, and the Florida Supreme Court ordered one to proceed, setting a deadline of December twelfth.

The U.S. Supreme Court, in Bush v. Gore, halted Florida's recount on Fourteenth Amendment equal protection grounds, finding that varying counting standards violated equal protection. The decision was five-to-four along ideological lines; critics argued the majority was result-oriented, choosing an unprecedented ground to decide the case. Bush won Florida's twenty-five electors and the presidency. His presidency would encompass nine-eleven and the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
